cards.answer: The bill passage model is the cleanest example, because I owned every step. I framed it as a survival problem: most bills die at different procedural stages, and "will this pass" depends on when you ask. Action text was unlabeled, so I built a 47-category taxonomy and labeled 1.39 million action rows. I applied a leakage guard at one point before aggregation, expanded each bill into prefixes so the model learns from every point in its life, and split train and test at the bill level. The production model is TF-IDF into a HistGradientBoostingClassifier, rescored daily by a scheduled pipeline. Validation came last and changed the most. After a corpus correction and retraining, on a held-out General Assembly it reached 75.1% precision and 76.2% recall at a 0.70 threshold, with a median 21 days' warning.

cards.answer: The feature that moved the most was the bill itself. My introduction-time model scores a bill before any procedural history exists, and on the held-out 103rd General Assembly it sat at a near-chance ROC-AUC of 0.561. Adding each bill's title and synopsis raised it to 0.845. A jump that size makes me suspicious before it makes me happy, so I confirmed it with an ablation study and three leakage checks. The other half of feature work is removal. In the retirement model I retired the macroeconomic features: unemployment and market indices are identical for every employee in a run, so they can't change anyone's rank in a report whose whole purpose is ranking, and across 21 annual anchors they mostly let the model dress a year effect up as a market effect.

cards.answer: I validate the way the model will be used, which almost always means out of time. For bill prediction I held out an entire General Assembly, the 103rd, and split at the bill level so a bill's early actions can't sit in training while its later ones are tested. I also built safeguards so no prediction made after the outcome was known gets counted. For the retirement model, panel data of that shape must never be split at random, so splits are by anchor year only. The risk-band cut points were fitted on 2019 to 2022, frozen, then applied untouched to 2023 to 2025, and checked seven more ways by leaving one year out at a time. The Elevated band had the higher retirement rate in all seven.

cards.answer: I pick the metric that answers the stakeholder's real question, then report it against the right baseline. For bill prediction, nobody acts on an AUC. They want to know how often a call is right and how much warning it gives, so the headline is precision and recall at a 0.70 threshold plus median days of warning. For rare events I lead with PR-AUC, because ROC-AUC can look flattering when negatives dominate. The retirement model's PR-AUC is 0.182, which only means something next to a 0.024 base rate. I still use ROC-AUC where ranking is the point, as with the introduction-time bill model. And I distrust any metric without a denominator: the legacy retirement report quoted a hit rate with no false-positive count, which is close to guaranteed when you flag 12.6% of staff.

cards.answer: I treat ranking and calibration as separate claims, because a model can order people well and still print the wrong numbers. In the inherited retirement report, out-of-time testing showed the top bin predicting 42.5% where 5.6% actually retired, even though the model ranked a retiree above a non-retiree roughly 85% of the time. Stakeholders were reading those percentages literally. I replaced them with two observed-rate risk bands, Elevated at 6.3% and Lower at 0.4%, each with a 95% confidence interval. The rebuilt pipeline uses a rank-based calibration layer, and I caught that it washed out a probability floor applied before it, so the floor now runs after calibration, on the printed scale. My bill-model validation checked calibration with ECE, and the app says plainly that its probabilities rank well but run overconfident.

cards.answer: I put an interval on any comparison I'm going to act on, and I match the test to how the data is paired. In my document-intelligence evaluation every model answered the same frozen questions, so comparisons are paired: paired bootstrap intervals for effect sizes, McNemar tests for right-or-wrong outcomes, and Holm correction because I was testing many methods at once. When I later confirmed parsers, the bootstrap was clustered by source, since items from the same source are correlated. The pre-registered method, majority-of-three voting, gained 4.5 points on a 7B model with a 95% interval of 3.0 to 6.1. For proportions from small samples I use Wilson intervals and gate on the lower bound; one precision check passed at 84 of 96, 87.5%. The retirement risk bands carry 95% intervals too.

cards.answer: I design experiments so they can't reach a convenient conclusion by accident, and to be straight, my experiments have been offline evaluations, not live A/B tests on user traffic. The discipline carries over. In my document-intelligence work I froze the cases and fingerprinted every request, then pre-registered majority-of-three voting as the single confirmatory method before running the held-out set. Failed or truncated answers stayed in the denominator as zeros, and nothing was re-run to rescue a result. For the vLLM throughput study I changed one variable at a time, holding prompt design, concurrency and serving stack fixed in turn, then added a same-model control. When a vendor model scored badly, I reassessed it one mechanism at a time across 192 requests before concluding anything.

cards.answer: Small data mostly changes what I'm allowed to claim. The retirement panel has 4,891 person-year rows but only about 101 to 118 retirements, so I sized the design to the events. A three-band version looked better in-sample and collapsed under prospective testing, so the report uses two bands, and I documented that as a limit of the event count. The 75-and-over cell had zero retirements across 26 person-years, which is why I shrank those estimates toward an age-based prior. The production run aborts if the panel returns fewer than 30 positives. Evaluation sets get the same scrutiny: 80 pages couldn't rule out a 0.02 numeric-recall deficit, so a promising model counted as a lead, not a win. When pooling is possible I measure it: wider System Office data moved PR-AUC from 0.182 to 0.199.

cards.answer: I use survival framing whenever the question is about when, and the retirement forecast is the clearest case. I built annual point-in-time snapshots from 2005 onward and labeled each active person forward twelve months, a survival-style panel. For people beyond the data's support, I fitted an age-based separation hazard to published labor-force participation anchors, with a Gompertz mortality component as a floor on involuntary exit. Across 21 years, the hazard by age plus service showed Rule-of-85 eligibility behaving as a window: risk peaks approaching 85, at 19% for 80 to 85, and declines afterward. The roadmap models all departures under a competing-risks framing, roughly three times the data. Bill prediction uses the same framing; Cox proportional hazards is recorded there as future work, not something I've shipped.

questions: empirical bayes

cards.answer: I reach for empirical-Bayes shrinkage when a group is too small for its own estimate to be trusted. In the retirement model, a random forest returns near zero wherever it has no comparable training cases, and the 75-and-over cell had zero retirements across 26 person-years. The result was indefensible: a 74-year-old with 39 years of service scored below a 58-year-old. I built an age-adjustment module that shrinks estimates toward an age-based separation hazard, sets a floor at 60% of the age-implied hazard, counts comparable cases for each person, and caps the age-plus-service value at the range the training data supports. Every person's output shows the raw score, the prior, the support count, the shrunk value, the floor and which mechanism moved it, so a changed number can be explained from evidence.

cards.answer: Most of my forecasting has been institutional time series with short histories, so I keep the models simple and check where they fail. For UIC enrollment, my team built ARIMA models per college and student level across 14 colleges, with orders chosen by grid search and later by Auto-ARIMA on AIC and BIC. Splitting the data into Fall, Spring and Summer series removed seasonality from each one. For 12 combinations where ARIMA wouldn't give a reliable forecast, we used Holt's double exponential smoothing, sweeping alpha and beta on an 80/20 split and picking by validation RMSE. Forecasts went out as a point estimate plus or minus validation MAE. On the legislative platform, trend analysis uses 5-year monthly baselines with seasonal adjustment, regression-based trend modeling and directional momentum.

cards.answer: When I inherited the retirement-risk model, the central defect was that its "Probability of Retirement" column was never a probability. It was an ordinal ranking on an inflated scale, and out-of-time testing showed the top bin predicting 42.5% where 5.6% retired. Its headline hit rate had no denominator, no false-positive count and no held-out evaluation. Its features included macro indicators that couldn't change anyone's rank, and two incompatible service-year definitions meant age as of today could mix with service as of some other date. Downstream, a "75% rule" put 19 people in all three planning windows at once. I rebuilt it on a point-in-time panel with time-based splits, replaced the column with observed-rate bands, and told stakeholders plainly that individual values would change.

cards.answer: Train/serve skew is the first thing I check when a validated model behaves oddly in production, because the model can be fine while its inputs aren't. In the bill pipeline, nightly scoring formatted model input differently from training. I moved both onto one shared input module and verified 36,028 inputs byte-identical. I also regenerated the full probability trail, 1,275,296 scores, and checked it against production at a 0.99 correlation. Reproducibility gets the same treatment: fixed seeds, versioned model files with the recency half-life persisted into the artifact and the manifest, pinned dependency versions in the technical reference, and SQL under version control. Earlier, a production join silently matched only about 8,820 of 50,501 bills because two sources used different ID spaces; bill_number is now a stable second key.

cards.answer: The worst missing data is missing systematically and quietly. While validating the bill model, I found the training corpus was missing every resolved bill, traced to a status filter; passed-bill coverage was 1.2%. I rebuilt the corpus from 46,815 to 117,722 bills and 1,444,601 action records, reaching 100% coverage, and separated resolutions from bills, which moved the apparent success rate from 30.4% to a true 13.2%. The retirement work was reconstruction from scratch: the training set had never existed, so I built annual point-in-time snapshots with effective-dated reads at every anchor. Where I can't fill a gap, I keep it visible. Failed model answers stay in the denominator as zeros, and four report cells I couldn't reproduce are documented rather than forced to agree.

cards.answer: I use unsupervised methods mostly to find structure I didn't know to label, then hand the result to a person or a downstream rule. In the bill taxonomy work, I clustered the uncategorized remainder with TF-IDF and KMeans to name the themes the taxonomy was missing. That made coverage an iterative loop: review clusters, update the taxonomy, re-run, measure the delta. It reached 99.0%. On a 20-year email archive, LDA on subject lines found five themes, and Llama turned keyword clusters into readable topic titles; re-running on LLM summaries with 10 topics surfaced HR and compliance themes the subject lines hid. For the HR proof of concept, built on a synthetic 500-employee dataset, I designed graph community detection with NetworkX greedy modularity to find career families and hub roles.

cards.answer: For predictive text features I start with sparse, inspectable representations and add semantic ones where they earn their place. The production bill model uses TF-IDF on action text, 1 to 2 grams, min_df 5, max_df 0.95, sublinear term frequency and 50,000 features, into gradient boosting. Cleaning matters as much as the vectorizer: in California, journal page numbers and legislator names were dominating the feature space until I stripped them. For research proposals I fused TF-IDF, KeyBERT and LDA keywords, since each catches what the others miss. Embeddings handle similarity: MiniLM with FAISS for archive and legislative search, bge-small over six million procurement rows. The introduction-time model leans on LLM-extracted bill semantics, and adding title and synopsis raised its held-out ROC-AUC from 0.561 to 0.845.

cards.title: Gradient boosting, random forest or logistic regression

cards.answer: I choose by data shape and by what the model has to explain. For the bill model, 50,000 sparse TF-IDF features on action-sequence prefixes suit histogram gradient boosting: it handles interactions and stays deterministic with a fixed seed. For the retirement panel, a few thousand rows of person features, I used a 500-tree random forest, then hit its known weakness: it returns near zero wherever no comparable case exists, so it needed an age prior. Logistic regression is my interpretable baseline and fallback; the HR departure-risk design pairs it with XGBoost and falls back to eligibility and tenure rules if performance is insufficient. At UIC, H2O's random forest beat CatBoost on the class that mattered, discontinuing students. I've also run TF-IDF with KNN, logistic regression and random forest for job classification.

cards.answer: I tune in proportion to what the data can support, and I keep the search honest by validating it out of sample. For Holt's smoothing at UIC we swept alpha and beta from 0.05 to 1.0 in steps of 0.05, picked the pair with the lowest validation RMSE on an 80/20 split, then refit on all the data. ARIMA orders came from grid search, later Auto-ARIMA on AIC and BIC. For the bill model I kept a conservative, documented spec: 150 iterations, max depth 6, learning rate 0.1, min_samples_leaf 20, fixed seed. Some of the most consequential settings aren't model hyperparameters at all. I chose a 730-day recency half-life over a 5-year window with recorded reasoning, and I treated risk-band cut points as tuned parameters, frozen before testing.

cards.answer: I treat fairness as something to design and test, and I'll be precise about how far I've taken it. For the HR workforce platform I designed an equity audit view that checks whether succession and promotion recommendations are proportionally distributed across demographic groups, with top-K candidate lists reviewed for representation balance and a formal fairness review scheduled in the validation phase. That was a proof of concept on synthetic data mirroring the HR tables, so I haven't yet audited a production model on real demographic data. In production, my equity work has been about not misleading people about individuals: refusing to let retirement-risk output be labeled "projected retirements", and escalating whether the report should rank people who resemble past retirees as a business decision instead of settling it myself.

cards.answer: I monitor the inputs, the outputs and the monitor itself. The bill model runs on two clocks: a daily rescore of active bills and a monthly retrain with recency weighting, so prediction freshness and model freshness can't be confused. Pipelines write structured logs that a job execution monitor I built reads, and it alerts on failures, cascades and pipelines that go silent. The retirement pipeline validates its output against a frozen contract of 4 files, 21 sheets and 436 columns on every run, and aborts if the panel returns fewer than 30 positives. The defect that mattered most wasn't caught by a metric: stalled bills holding their peak probability showed up only once the trail was exposed. I haven't shipped a formal distribution-drift alarm; recency weighting and scheduled retraining are how I handle drift today.

cards.answer: For anomaly detection I prefer simple, explainable baselines that an analyst can check by hand. On the legislative platform, trend analysis compares activity against 5-year monthly baselines, seasonally adjusted, and flags unusual movement with Z-score anomaly detection, alongside regression-based trend modeling and directional momentum. Adjusting for season first matters, because legislative activity has a strong calendar. At the bill level, a momentum badge compares a bill's probability over its last three actions against the prior three and labels it Gaining, Stable or Losing. I apply the same idea to pipeline health: the job monitor flags a pipeline as silent when hours since its last success pass a threshold, and I set that to 100 days for a quarterly pipeline, which would otherwise breach the standard 48-hour rule two days after every run.

questions: markov chain simulation

cards.answer: I've used Markov chains for career mobility, and it's proof-of-concept work. For the HR workforce platform, the proof of concept I led with intern collaborators built a career transition matrix from each employee's historical job-title sequence, giving the conditional probability of every next role from any starting role. A simulation engine walks those transitions stochastically and summarizes many simulated paths into a distribution of where people in a role land after N moves, for example where academic advisors end up after four moves, shown as a Sankey flow. The same matrix feeds graph analytics that classify dead-end, feeder and fast-track roles. It ran on a synthetic 500-employee dataset mirroring the HR tables. On real data, the first thing to validate is the Markov assumption that the next move depends only on the current role; the build plan schedules validation against historical trends.

cards.answer: At scale I design for vectorized passes and cheap lookups before I write a loop. Labeling 1,388,400 legislative action rows one at a time with fuzzy matching wouldn't have been runnable, so I wrote a two-pass labeler: combined regex patterns via str.contains across the whole column resolve roughly 85 to 90% of rows in under 30 seconds, then rapidfuzz partial_ratio runs only on the remainder. Final coverage was 99.65%. For procurement, a per-query DataFrame scan took about 1,700 ms, so I built an in-memory dictionary keyed on manufacturer and part number with itertuples: about 90 seconds at startup, then under 2 ms per lookup across six million rows. On the SQL side, I externalize queries into version-controlled files with shared cohort CTEs and effective-dated reads.

cards.answer: I communicate uncertainty as observed rates and plain statements people can repeat accurately. For the retirement report I replaced a fake probability with two bands and their real outcomes: in the Elevated band 6.3% retired within the year, with a 95% interval of 3.9 to 10.2, against 0.4% in the Lower band. I proposed a multi-year framing with the stakeholder, so leadership can say something defensible like a one-in-four chance of retiring within four years. I also said what the output may not be called: "projected retirements". For bill prediction I standardized one phrase, floor-vote likelihood, after finding five descriptions in the app, because someone who reads "passage" next to 94% has misunderstood before reading any documentation. UIC forecasts went out with a plus-or-minus MAE band.

cards.answer: I'll be direct: I haven't run a formal causal study in production, such as a randomized trial or a difference-in-differences design on institutional data. The closest work is regression analysis at the San Diego Regional Data Library, quantifying differences in economic indicators between Special Economic Zone and non-zone regions, with nighttime light intensity as a proxy for economic activity. Day to day, causal thinking shows up as attribution discipline. When vLLM delivered a 6.22x speedup, I re-ran the old backend on the same model architecture to split it into 3.6x from serving and about 1.7x from the model swap. I confirm feature gains with ablations, and I keep stakeholders from reading prediction as cause: the retirement output ranks people who resemble past retirees, which is different from forecasting who will leave.

cards.answer: I evaluate LLM output like any other measurement problem: fix the bar first, sample deliberately, and report the lower bound. In Skyrule, my personal project, exhaustive grading of a 2.6-million-piece generated library would have cost about 5,600 GPU-hours, so I designed lot acceptance sampling with exact binomial plans and stated producer and consumer risk, plus code checks on every piece. Quality bars are set before measurement and reported as a point estimate and a Wilson 95% lower bound. Judges get validated too: an independent model labels claims, I measure its agreement with my own verdicts, and those labels become a regression set for the validator. In my document-intelligence evaluation, no model grades another; published answer keys and code do the scoring, and failures count as zeros.

cards.answer: A simple model is enough when it answers the decision and the extra complexity can't be validated. The bill model is TF-IDF plus gradient boosting on action-sequence prefixes. I recorded Cox proportional hazards, LSTMs and DeepSurv as an upgrade path, and documented the current approach as a deliberate baseline chosen for interpretability and production tractability. The retirement report uses two risk bands because a three-band version collapsed prospectively, and I retired macro features that added a manual quarterly chore without changing anyone's rank. In procurement, exact matching on manufacturer and part number confirmed 42,052 identical products with no AI at all; embeddings and an LLM only see what's left. A more complex method has to win out of sample before it replaces a simple one.

cards.answer: I spend more time on the target definition than on the model, because a wrong target gives a confident answer to the wrong question. For retirement risk, each annual anchor captures who was active on that date and labels them forward twelve months, with the last anchor a full year before the run so an absent retirement is a true negative. I documented the boundary cost: 4 of 122 retirements fall on the wrong side of a January-to-January window, which makes recall slightly pessimistic. At UIC we built four label variants and recommended binary success, since graduation and continuation look more like each other than like dropout. For bills, Stage 2 predicts reaching a floor vote, not becoming law, and in California I redefined the target to floor votes only.

cards.answer: Honestly, I haven't built a stacked meta-learner in production. My ensemble work takes three other forms. Tree ensembles are my default for tabular data: H2O's distributed random forest at UIC and a 500-tree random forest for retirement risk. At the output level, my document-intelligence evaluation pre-registered majority-of-three voting as its confirmatory method. It held for a 7B model at plus 4.5 points and for a 32B at plus 2.6, with no reliable gain on the 8B, so it's worth its triple cost only for some models. For features, my research-proposal pipeline fuses TF-IDF, KeyBERT and LDA keywords into one profile. At UIC we documented class-sensitive ensembles for the discontinued segment as a future recommendation.

cards.answer: I staged the bill model because each point in a bill's life supports a different question. Stage 1 scores a bill at introduction, when the only signal is the bill itself. It's the hardest stage, and adding title and synopsis lifted its held-out ROC-AUC from 0.561 to 0.845. Stage 2 is the production model: given the procedural history so far, the likelihood the bill reaches a floor vote, rescored after every new action. Stage 3 predicts individual legislators' votes from vote history, party alignment and committee roles; it's trained but waiting on production feature integration before it joins the daily loop. Stage 1 activates on the server when its model file is present, with no pipeline code changes. I sequenced it with Stage 2 live and scoring daily while Stages 1 and 3 were staged for integration.

cards.answer: Most of my label sets didn't exist until I built them, so I treat label quality as something to measure. For legislative actions I labeled 1.39 million rows with procedural stage and activity type at 99.65% coverage, keeping the raw labeled history for inspection, and in California an iterative audit of unlabeled actions drove taxonomy updates. When there's no ground truth, I say so: my LLM extraction evaluation used a blind three-criterion rubric and reported no ROC curve, because rubric scores are expert judgments. I quantify boundary noise too: 4 of 122 retirement labels fall on the wrong side of the window. For institutional documents, the planned readiness gate is a human-labeled set of about 100 documents with 20 double-labeled, so agreement between labelers can be measured instead of assumed.

cards.title: Statistics fundamentals: overfitting, bias-variance, p-values

cards.answer: I'd explain them through mistakes I've caught. Overfitting is a model learning the sample instead of the pattern; my clearest case is a three-band retirement design that looked better in-sample and collapsed prospectively, its middle band scoring below its bottom band. That's bias versus variance in practice: with roughly a hundred events, a finer model carries more variance than the data can pay for, so I accepted the coarser two-band version. A p-value is the probability of a result at least as extreme if there were no real effect, which is why testing many methods inflates false wins and why I apply Holm correction. And I watch effective sample size: recency weights are normalized to mean 1 so weighting doesn't quietly shrink the data.

cards.answer: I treat a near-perfect score as a bug report until proven otherwise, and I check four things in order. First, the target: in California the first definition counted committee votes, a 76.4% positive rate that made the task trivial, so I redefined it as floor votes only. Second, the population: my June bill model's corpus was missing every resolved bill through a status filter, and resolutions pooled with bills had inflated the success rate to 30.4% from a true 13.2%. Third, leakage and splits: outcome terms audited, bill-level splits, a full Assembly held out, and an ablation for any big feature gain. Fourth, individual behavior, because aggregates hide things: the per-action trail showed stalled bills keeping their peak probability. After the fixes I replaced the June headline with held-out results.

cards.answer: Precision at a threshold matches how the model is used: an analyst sees a flagged bill and wants to know how often a flag is right. At 0.70 on the held-out 103rd General Assembly, 75.1% of the bills the model flagged were correct calls, it caught 76.2% of the bills it should have, and the median first call came 21 days before the floor vote. The warning measure needs safeguards so no prediction made after the outcome is counted. The 0.70 itself isn't a tuned optimum. I picked it as an illustrative operating point, to show how much lead time you get at a given level of certainty, and the validation results in the platform let you choose your own threshold and see the lead time and accuracy that come with it. The right threshold depends on how many flags a team can review. And it's one held-out Assembly, which I report as such, not a long prospective record.

cards.answer: I keep a twelve-item limitations document, and four failure modes matter most. First, Stage 2 predicts reaching a floor vote, not becoming law; bills reach votes and fail, so the app says floor-vote likelihood everywhere. Second, the probability trail misbehaves after a stall: a bill that advanced and then stalled keeps its peak probability. The real fix is a decay term on time since the last advancing action plus down-weighting on re-referral, and the display patch is documented as insufficient. Third, probabilities rank well but run overconfident in absolute terms. Fourth, the evidence is one held-out Assembly, not a long prospective record. Open model work includes unifying the labeler and verifying synopses against as-introduced bill text, since Stage 1 now leans on them.

cards.answer: The biggest issue is a feature. TOTAL_COMPLETED_TERMS was the top predictor, and in October 2026 I added a correction to the case study: it counts terms across all recorded history, so it can partly reveal the outcome, and the selected model's cross-validated scores may be inflated by leakage. I'd rebuild with features computed strictly as of each snapshot, the way my retirement panel reads effective-dated rows. Second, performance varied by term: Cohen's kappa was 0.882 for Fall but 0.461 for Spring, where dropout patterns are more diffuse. Third, the SMOTE step ran without a static seed, so runs weren't deterministic. And predicted discontinued counts consistently ran under actuals, which needed an adjustment ratio. We documented those limits and recommended domain-informed feature selection.

cards.answer: The biggest blind spot is announced retirements: someone who has given notice looks identical to someone with no plans until HR processes the termination. The fix is an HR-maintained list of known intent, shown as Confirmed instead of predicted, which also makes the remaining predictions more honest. Next, I'd model all departures under a competing-risks framing, roughly three times the data and closer to what stakeholders actually ask. I'd persist the trained model so past quarters can be explained, publish the confidence column so thin-evidence cases are visible, and replace an inherited eligibility constant with confirmed SURS Tier I and Tier II rules. One question stays a business decision: whether the report ranks people who resemble past retirees or forecasts who will retire next year.

cards.answer: I measure a model by what it changes downstream, and I'm explicit about what can't be measured. For the rebuilt retirement-risk forecast, which Strategic Workforce Planning uses each quarter, I track three things. Delivery: the outstanding report shipped the same day the old system's loss surfaced, and the pipeline now runs quarterly in about six minutes. Decision quality: observed-rate bands with roughly fifteen-fold separation, plus a planning workbook placing 73 employees at the earliest horizon they enter the Elevated band, each exactly once. Errors removed: the old 75% rule had 19 people in all three windows at once. What I can't claim is that it's more accurate than the original, which no longer exists to compare against. What I can claim is that it's auditable where the original wasn't.

cards.answer: When older data is still informative but the world has shifted, I weight it instead of cutting it. For the bill model I compared a rolling 5-year training window against exponential decay and chose decay. The procedural grammar of the legislature is stable across 16 years, so a 5-year cut would discard roughly half the data for no gain; what shifts is the base rate and political salience of categories. I implemented decay as sample weights with a 730-day half-life, so a 2022 bill counts about half as much as a 2024 bill and a 2018 bill about 10%, normalized to mean 1 to preserve effective sample size. The half-life is stored in both the model artifact and the manifest, and a monthly retrain refreshes the model on full history.

iv-leakage.answer: I assume leakage until I've ruled it out, especially when a number looks great. In bill prediction, procedural history leaks by construction: the actions that record a bill passing live in the same table as the actions that predict it. So I remove outcome-revealing stages at a single point before aggregation, split at the bill level, and keep the raw labeled history so the guard can be inspected rather than trusted. The title-and-synopsis gain was confirmed with an ablation and three leakage checks before I published it. In California, the first target counted committee votes, which made the task trivially easy; I redefined it as floor votes only. In the retirement panel every historical read is effective-dated. At UIC, two top-ranked variables were term-dependent leakage and were dropped.

iv-class-imbalance.answer: With rare events I decide whether to rebalance at all, then make sure evaluation still reflects the real base rate. The retirement panel has about 101 to 118 positive events in 4,891 person-year rows, a 2.4% base rate, so I report PR-AUC against that base rate and precision and recall at every candidate threshold instead of accuracy. For bill prediction I trained on a class-balanced sample capped at 100,000 rows per class, and evaluated on a held-out General Assembly. At UIC, the team applied SMOTE to the 70% training partition only, never the 30% test set, so synthetic minority rows couldn't inflate the evaluation. And when events are this thin, I let them limit the design: the retirement report uses two risk bands because three couldn't hold up prospectively.

iv-precision-vs-recall.answer: I treat the operating threshold as a business decision that I inform with the full trade-off. For the retirement report I reported precision and recall at every candidate threshold and handed flag volume to stakeholders as what it actually is: a decision about how many people leadership is willing to review. For bill prediction, at 0.70 on a held-out General Assembly the model gives 75.1% precision and 76.2% recall with a median 21 days' warning, and warning time is part of the trade-off, since a model that becomes confident the morning of the vote is accurate and useless. In relevance scoring, when a speed-limit bill surfaced as high impact to an AI-ethics reader because of an incidental camera provision, I flagged threshold tightening instead of shipping a tenuous inference to a sophisticated audience.

iv-choose-between-models.answer: I decide what failure costs before I compare, then let that criterion pick. At UIC the institutional use was finding students likely to discontinue, so error on that class decided it: H2O's random forest kept error below 5% across all three classes in cross-validation, while CatBoost's error on the Discontinued class was 47.71% with a systematic residual. For legislative extraction, the job was 11,673 bills and roughly 155 unattended hours, so I weighted stability over peak: Mistral at 500 tokens swung 0.10 in rubric score across chunk sizes against 0.35 for Qwen, even though Qwen had the higher single score. And I re-run the comparison when conditions change. After the vLLM migration, production moved to Llama 3.1 8B because the recovered headroom made the larger model affordable.

iv-interpretable-models.answer: I build interpretability for the person who has to argue with the model, and I check the explanation method itself for artifacts. For bill prediction I ranked survival and death signals by presence versus absence, then found every survival signal scoring about 0.297, because long winning bills share many tokens. I specified a dual method that adds the model's own TF-IDF weights times feature importances, rather than ship a chart ordered by a metric artifact. The retirement report gives each person their raw score, age prior, comparable-case count, shrunk estimate, floor, final value and a confidence rating. At UIC we used variable importance, SHAP and partial dependence plots. And the bill app shows the score after every action, so a jump from 46% to 85% on "Do Pass" is legible.
